title: Wald and score tests
dek: Three first-order equivalent tests: LRT uses both fits, Wald uses the full fit, score uses only the restricted fit. Finite samples pick a favourite, especially near boundaries.
story: The trinity: LRT = 2(ℓ₁ − ℓ₀). Wald = (θ̂ − θ₀)ᵀ J(θ̂) (θ̂ − θ₀). Score = S(θ₀)ᵀ I(θ₀)⁻¹ S(θ₀). Under regularity they share a χ²_k limit. They are not the same number in your GLM output.

Wald needs the unrestricted MLE and a covariance at that point. If θ̂ exploded (separation) or se is junk, Wald is junk. Score needs only the restricted fit — attractive when the alternative is messy (extra random effect, extra mixture component).

Near 0/1 probabilities, Wald intervals from logit models are the ones that overshoot the parameter space. Score (Wilson) intervals for a single proportion are the textbook repair. The same geometry shows up in multiparameter GLMs.
deepTitle: Which χ², and when they quarrel
deep: Geometry: LRT is a comparison of heights of ℓ. Wald is a comparison of θ̂ to θ₀ in a quadratic approximation at θ̂. Score is a check of whether the slope at θ₀ is too big for a mean-zero score. If ℓ is quadratic they coincide. If ℓ is skewed they do not.
Robust Wald replaces J or I with a sandwich. There is no equally standard “sandwich LRT.” If you committed to sandwich SEs, the matching test is Wald (or a robust score).

Boundary: testing τ = 0, the score test can be set up with a one-sided reference; Wald is awkward because θ̂ piles at 0; LRT uses a mixture of χ². Software stars are often the wrong member of the trinity.

Degrees of freedom are the number of restrictions, as in Wilks. A Wald test of two coefficients jointly is χ²_2, not two starred t tests. Look at the covariance: highly correlated β̂s can be jointly significant or jointly null in ways the margins hide.

formulas.label: Wald
formulas.note: Uses the unrestricted fit. z = β̂/se is the 1-df case.

formulas.label: Score / Lagrange multiplier
formulas.note: Uses the restricted fit only. Pearson χ² for a proportion is a score test.

visual.caption: Same nested pair, three readings of ℓ. LRT: vertical gap between peaks. Wald: horizontal distance from θ̂ to the restriction, scaled by curvature at θ̂. Score: slope at the restriction, scaled by curvature there.

example.title: Testing a proportion against 0.05
example.setup: n = 40, y = 0 high-confidence BDQ mutations. H₀: π = 0.05. Compare Wald, score, LRT for a Bernoulli model.

steps.title: MLE
steps.body: π̂ = 0. Wald statistic uses se at 0, which is 0. W is undefined or insane. This is the separation/boundary cousin for a single proportion.

steps.title: Score
steps.body: Under H₀, se₀ = √(0.05×0.95/40) ≈ 0.034. Score uses (π̂ − 0.05)/se₀. With π̂ = 0 this is a finite number. Pearson form is the usual textbook version.

steps.title: LRT
steps.body: Λ = 2(ℓ(0) − ℓ(0.05)) needs care at π̂ = 0 because log 0. The binomial likelihood at 0 is (1−π)^n, so ℓ(0.05) = 40 log 0.95, ℓ(π̂) = 0 in the extended sense. Finite, skewed, honest.

example.takeaway: When θ̂ sits on a wall, prefer score or LRT (or Bayes). Wald assumed an interior peak.

check.prompt: The score test is computationally attractive when:
choices: The alternative model is hard to maximise, but the null model is easy
You only have the unrestricted MLE
check.answer: The alternative model is hard to maximise, but the null model is easy
check.why: Score uses S(θ₀) from the restricted fit. Extra variance components and extra mixture terms are the usual case.

whyWrong.n is infinite by assumption: Asymptotics are shared; the finite-sample appeal is computational.

check.prompt: β̂ = 2, se = 1, H₀: β = 0. Wald z equals:
check.why: z = β̂/se = 2. W = z² = 4 would be the χ²_1 form — not asked.

whyWrong.0: The null value, not the statistic.

check.prompt: On the trinity plate, Wald is described as using curvature at θ̂. That fails when:
check.figureHint: Full box: Wald uses curvature here.
choices: θ̂ is infinite or the Hessian at θ̂ is degenerate, so the quadratic at the peak is a bad or missing object
The null is easy to fit
check.answer: θ̂ is infinite or the Hessian at θ̂ is degenerate, so the quadratic at the peak is a bad or missing object
check.why: Separation, boundary MLEs, singular I. Score looks at the null instead.
